S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor occurring within three months of the onset of that stressor. The reaction is considered clinically significant because it is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor and/or causes marked impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, but does not meet criteria for another mental disorder. Symptoms typically resolve within six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended, and the course is usually time-limited, though it can become chronic if the stressor is ongoing. It is distinguished from normal stress reactions by the degree of distress and functional impairment, and from other disorders such as Major Depressive Disorder or PTSD by its temporal relationship to the stressor, symptom severity, and absence of a more specific syndromic pattern.

patient.personality: Marta is an organized, community‑oriented planner who thrives on structure, social connection, and hands‑on involvement in church and local events, despite some mild personal disorganization in her own errands and collections.
patient.stressor: Roughly four and a half months ago, Marta’s adult daughter and two young grandchildren moved back into her home after a sudden marital separation, turning Marta and her husband’s relatively calm household into a crowded, emotionally charged space. Marta quickly stepped into a caregiving and problem‑solving role—coordinating legal appointments, school transitions, and childcare—while still trying to keep up her extensive church volunteering and event consulting commitments. Over the following weeks, simmering tensions between her daughter and son‑in‑law, financial worries about supporting an extra household, and conflicts with her husband over boundaries gradually eroded the predictable routines and community activities that usually kept her grounded. When she began canceling long‑standing quilting circles and church events, snapping at people during planning meetings, and feeling overwhelmed by even small decisions at home, her pastor and a close friend encouraged her to see a psychiatrist to help her cope with how intensely she was reacting to the family upheaval.
patient.chief_complaint: “Since my daughter and the kids moved back after her marriage fell apart, I feel like I’m not coping well with all the stress at home and it’s throwing everything in my life off.”

S081.manifestation: Ever since my daughter and the kids moved back in, it feels like this whole situation has taken over my mind and my moods—one minute I’m teary and guilty that I’m not doing enough for everyone, the next I’m snapping at my husband over something small, canceling church things I used to love because I just feel too wound up and overwhelmed to deal with one more person needing something from me.
